forbidden_claims.statement_nl: Let $n$ be an integer greater than 1. For which real numbers $x$ is \\[\\lfloor nx \\rfloor - \\sum_{k=1}^{n} \\frac{\\lfloor kx \\rfloor}{k}\\] maximal, and what is the maximal value that this expression can take?

payload.previous_feedback: Previous vetter reason: The proof exactly matches the lemma statement: for arbitrary real x, it defines m = floor(x) and f = x - m, then verifies m is an integer, x = m + f, and 0 <= f < 1. This is the standard floor/fractional-part decomposition and is complete with no semantic drift.
payload.previous_proof_nl: Let x be an arbitrary real number. Set m = floor(x). By definition of the floor function, m is an integer and m <= x < m + 1. Define f = x - m. Then f >= 0 because x >= m, and f < 1 because x < m + 1. Also, by the definition of fractional part, frac(x) = x - floor(x) = x - m = f. Hence x = m + f = floor(x) + frac(x), and 0 <= frac(x) < 1. Since x was arbitrary, the statement holds for every real x.

assumptions: frac(x) denotes the fractional part x-floor(x)

result_payload.proof_nl: Let x be any real number. By definition of the floor function, m := floor(x) is an integer such that m <= x < m + 1. Define f := x - m. Then f >= 0 because x >= m, and f < 1 because x < m + 1. By the usual definition of the fractional part, frac(x) = x - floor(x) = x - m = f. Therefore x = m + f = floor(x) + frac(x), and also 0 <= frac(x) < 1. Since x was arbitrary, the statement holds for every real number x.
result_payload.proof_summary: Use the defining property of floor: m=floor(x) satisfies m<=x<m+1. Setting f=x-m gives 0<=f<1, and f is exactly frac(x). Hence x=floor(x)+frac(x) with 0<=frac(x)<1 for all real x.

used_external_facts: Standard definition of the fractional part as frac(x)=x-floor(x).
